figures.title: The Protein Family Tree
figures.subtitle: Amino acids build up into peptides and proteins; food supplies the amino acids.

segments.name: What Protein Is
segments.text: Protein is the next macronutrient in this course. Like fat it gives energy, about four calories per gram, the same as carbohydrate. But energy isn't its main job. Protein is what your body is built from and what does most of its work: muscle, skin and hair, the enzymes that run every chemical reaction, the antibodies that fight infection, and the hemoglobin that carries oxygen in your blood.
segments.cue: Title, then the chain down the middle, from Amino acids to Protein

foodBody.name: Enzymes
foodBody.text: Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions without being used up. The lipases that break down fat in Fats Figure 9 are enzymes, and so are pepsin and trypsin, which digest protein in Figure 6.

foodBody.name: Antibodies
foodBody.text: Antibodies are Y-shaped immune proteins that latch onto germs and tag them for your immune system to destroy. Eating enough protein, plus zinc from foods like meat, shellfish and seeds, supports making them.

foodBody.name: Hemoglobin
foodBody.text: Hemoglobin is the iron-containing protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. Your body builds it from dietary protein plus iron, from foods like red meat, liver, beans and spinach.

segments.name: Amino Acids
segments.text: Every protein is built from smaller units called amino acids, the box at the top. There are twenty of them. Nine are essential, meaning your body can't make them, so they have to come from food. The other eleven your body can make, although six of those, called conditionally essential, can run short when you're ill, injured or growing fast.
segments.cue: Top: Amino acids, then Essential, Non-essential and Conditional on the left

segments.name: Chains
segments.text: Follow the arrows down the middle. Amino acids link together with peptide bonds, one after another, into a chain. A short chain, up to about fifty amino acids, is called a peptide. A longer chain folds into a working shape and becomes a protein. A peptide and a protein are the same kind of chain, just different lengths. Folded proteins make up your muscle and work as enzymes, antibodies and hemoglobin.
segments.cue: Down the middle: peptide bonds, Peptide, Protein, then the four boxes underneath

segments.name: Protein in Food
segments.text: On the right is food, where the amino acids come from. The protein you eat is digested back down into amino acids, the dashed arrow, and your body rebuilds them into its own proteins. A complete protein has all nine essential amino acids in good amounts. An incomplete one is low in at least one, but two incomplete proteins can cover each other's gaps. Each box links to the figure that explains it.
segments.cue: Right: Food, Complete, Incomplete, Combine them, and the dashed digestion arrow into Amino acids

segments.name: On the Label
segments.text: On a nutrition label, protein is just one line, in grams. In the US the percent Daily Value for protein is often left off; it's only required when the package makes a protein claim or the food is for young children. And the label won't tell you which amino acids are in there; Figure 7 shows how to tell from the food.
segments.cue: The three boxes under the tree

figures.title: From Atoms to an Amino Acid
figures.subtitle: Four kinds of atom, one shared backbone, one side chain that changes.

segments.name: Four Kinds of Atom
segments.text: Let's build an amino acid from scratch. It uses only a few kinds of atom, and each always makes the same number of bonds. Carbon makes four, like this methane. Nitrogen makes three, like ammonia. Oxygen makes two, like water. Hydrogen makes just one. Sulfur, which appears in two amino acids, makes two, like hydrogen sulfide.
segments.cue: The four small molecules, left to right

segments.name: Nitrogen Is New
segments.text: Fats and carbohydrates are made only of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. Protein adds nitrogen. That's the atom that makes protein special, and later we'll see that your body has to do something with it when protein is burned for energy.
segments.cue: Nitrogen (blue) in ammonia

segments.name: Glycine
segments.text: Here's the simplest amino acid, glycine. On the left is an amine group: a nitrogen with two hydrogens. That's the amino part of the name. In the middle is a carbon called the alpha carbon. On the right is a carboxyl group: a carbon with a double-bonded oxygen and an OH. That's the acid part, because the OH can give up its hydrogen.
segments.cue: Markers 1, 2, 3 on glycine

segments.name: The Side Chain
segments.text: Now alanine. It has exactly the same amine group, alpha carbon and carboxyl group. The only difference is what hangs off the alpha carbon. In glycine it's just a hydrogen; in alanine it's a CH3, a methyl group. That hanging part is called the side chain, or R group, and it's the only thing that differs between all twenty amino acids.
segments.cue: Marker 4: the side chain

segments.name: Charged in the Body
segments.text: One small detail: drawn here, the amine and carboxyl groups are neutral. In your body's fluids the carboxyl usually gives up its hydrogen and the amine picks one up, so each end carries a charge. The atoms are the same, just one hydrogen moved.

figures.title: The Peptide Bond
figures.subtitle: Amino acids join head to tail and release water.

segments.name: Head to Tail
segments.text: Amino acids join head to tail. The carboxyl group of one lines up with the amine group of the next. The OH from the carboxyl and one hydrogen from the amine come off together, and that's a water molecule, H2O.
segments.cue: Markers 1 and 2, then the water

segments.name: The Bond Itself
segments.text: What's left is a new bond between the carbon of the first amino acid and the nitrogen of the second. That carbon-nitrogen link, next to its C=O, is the peptide bond. It's strong and flat, which is part of why protein chains fold the way they do. Two amino acids joined like this make a dipeptide, here glycyl-alanine.
segments.cue: Marker 3: the peptide bond

segments.name: Adding More
segments.text: Add a third, here serine, and you get a tripeptide with two peptide bonds, and another water released. The chain always has a free amine at one end, called the N-terminus, and a free carboxyl at the other, the C-terminus. New amino acids are added at the C-terminus end.
segments.cue: N, markers 1 and 2, then C

segments.name: The Backbone
segments.text: Look along the chain: nitrogen, carbon, carbon, nitrogen, carbon, carbon. That repeating pattern is the backbone, and the side chains stick out from it, alternating sides. Most proteins are a few hundred amino acids long, some many thousands. Digestion is the reverse: water is added back to split each peptide bond.
segments.cue: The N–C–C repeat along the zigzag

figures.title: The 20 Amino Acids
figures.subtitle: Same backbone, 20 side chains; 9 you must eat.

segments.name: One Backbone, Twenty Side Chains
segments.text: Here are all twenty, drawn at the same scale and the same way round: the amine and carboxyl along the bottom, the side chain pointing up. The bottoms all match. Only the tops differ, from glycine's single hydrogen to tryptophan's big double ring.
segments.cue: Compare the bottoms, then the tops

segments.name: The Nine Essential
segments.text: These nine are essential: histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan and valine. Your body has no way to make their side chains, so every one has to come from food. Three of them, leucine, isoleucine and valine, have branched side chains and are called the branched-chain amino acids.
segments.cue: The nine marked essential

segments.name: Conditionally Essential
segments.text: The next six, arginine, cysteine, glutamine, glycine, proline and tyrosine, your body normally makes, but it can't always keep up, for example in premature babies, after serious injury or during illness. Some are made from essential ones: tyrosine from phenylalanine, and cysteine using the sulfur from methionine.
segments.cue: The six conditionally essential

segments.name: The Non-Essential Five
segments.text: The last five, alanine, asparagine, aspartic acid, glutamic acid and serine, your body makes easily from glucose and other amino acids. Non-essential doesn't mean unimportant; it only means you don't have to eat them.
segments.cue: The five non-essential

segments.name: What the Side Chains Do
segments.text: The side chains decide how a protein behaves. Oily ones like leucine and phenylalanine avoid water and end up inside a folded protein. Charged ones like lysine and glutamic acid face the water outside. Cysteine's sulfur can bond to another cysteine, a cross-link that holds shapes together, like the curls in hair.
segments.cue: The table: what each essential one does

segments.name: Raw Materials
segments.text: Some amino acids are also raw materials. Tryptophan becomes serotonin and melatonin, and a little niacin. Phenylalanine becomes tyrosine, which becomes adrenaline and the pigment melanin. Histidine becomes histamine. People with the inherited condition PKU can't process phenylalanine, which is why products with aspartame carry a phenylalanine warning.

figures.title: From Chain to Shape
figures.subtitle: Four levels of structure, and why cooking changes protein.

segments.name: Primary
segments.text: A protein's shape is described in four levels. The primary structure is simply the order of amino acids along the chain, drawn here as beads. That order is set by your genes, and it decides everything that follows. Change a single amino acid and the protein can change: sickle-cell hemoglobin differs from normal hemoglobin by just one.
segments.cue: Level 1: the bead chain

segments.name: Secondary
segments.text: Secondary structure is how short stretches coil or line up. The two common shapes are the alpha helix, a spiral, and the beta sheet, strands lying side by side. Both are held by hydrogen bonds: weak attractions between the C=O of one peptide bond and the N–H of another.
segments.cue: Level 2: the helix close-up (each C=O dashed to the N–H four along), then the sheet (C=O on one strand to N–H on the next)

segments.name: Tertiary
segments.text: Tertiary structure is the whole chain folded into its final shape. Oily side chains tuck inside, away from water, and water-loving ones face out, with a few sulfur cross-links holding it steady. The shape decides the job: an enzyme's pocket fits only the molecule it works on.
segments.cue: Level 3: the folded chain, then the close-up: oily side chains inside, water-loving outside, the two S–S links, and the enzyme-pocket inset

segments.name: Quaternary
segments.text: Some proteins are teams of chains, and that's quaternary structure. Hemoglobin is four chains, each holding a heme group with an iron atom that grabs oxygen. Collagen, the most common protein in your body, is three chains wound into a rope.
segments.cue: Level 4: hemoglobin (two alpha and two beta chains, each heme with its iron and O2), then the close-up of one heme in its pocket (iron in the flat ring, bent O2 above it, His E7 above, His F8 below, side view edge-on), then collagen's three-chain rope

foodBody.name: Hemoglobin
foodBody.text: Hemoglobin needs iron. Red meat, liver and shellfish give heme iron, which your body absorbs well; beans, lentils and spinach give non-heme iron, which is less well absorbed. Inside red blood cells, hemoglobin carries oxygen from your lungs to your tissues.

foodBody.name: Collagen
foodBody.text: Collagen comes from skin-on chicken, bone broth, gelatin and the connective tissue in meat. Your gut breaks it down to amino acids like any other protein, and your body builds its own collagen from them, using vitamin C. It is the main structural protein of skin, tendons, ligaments, bone and cartilage.

segments.name: Denaturing
segments.text: The folds are held by weak bonds, so heat, acid or whipping can undo them. That's denaturing. When egg white turns from clear to white, or milk curdles with lemon juice, the proteins are unfolding and tangling. The peptide bonds don't break, so the amino acids are all still there, and cooked protein is usually easier to digest.

figures.title: Digestion and Use
figures.subtitle: Back to amino acids, into the pool, and out as urea.

segments.name: In the Stomach
segments.text: Protein digestion starts in the stomach. Stomach acid denatures the proteins, unfolding them so enzymes can reach the peptide bonds, and an enzyme called pepsin starts cutting the chains into shorter pieces.
segments.cue: Mouth, then Stomach

segments.name: In the Small Intestine
segments.text: In the small intestine, the pancreas adds more enzymes, trypsin and chymotrypsin, and enzymes on the gut wall finish the job, down to single amino acids and some pairs and threes. These are absorbed into the blood and go first to the liver.
segments.cue: Small intestine, then Into the blood

segments.name: The Amino Acid Pool
segments.text: From there they join your body's amino acid pool, a supply that cells draw on all day. Your body breaks down and rebuilds a few hundred grams of its own protein every day, far more than you eat, and reuses most of the amino acids. Nothing is stored as spare protein, though, so you need a steady supply.
segments.cue: The amino acid pool

segments.name: What It Builds
segments.text: The pool builds muscle, skin, hair and the collagen in bone; enzymes; antibodies; carriers like hemoglobin; and hormones such as insulin. Only when there's more than you need for building are amino acids burned for energy, or turned into glucose or fat.
segments.cue: The three boxes

segments.name: Urea
segments.text: Burning an amino acid leaves its nitrogen behind as ammonia, which is toxic. Your liver joins two nitrogens with a carbon and an oxygen to make urea, this small molecule, and your kidneys send it out in urine. That's why a very high protein intake means a little more water.
segments.cue: Marker 1: the two nitrogens on urea; then the alanine diagram: the blue nitrogen lane (ammonia, urea, out in urine) and the grey carbon lane (pyruvate and its three fates)

segments.name: Too Little, Too Much
segments.text: Too little protein over time leads to muscle loss, slow healing, weaker immunity and thinning hair; in severe shortage, especially in children, swelling from fluid, a condition called kwashiorkor, and poor growth. Extra protein beyond your needs is burned or stored as fat; very high intakes are mainly a concern for people with kidney disease.

figures.title: Complete and Incomplete Protein
figures.subtitle: Which foods have all 9 essentials, and how to combine the rest.

segments.name: The Limiting Amino Acid
segments.text: Your body builds each protein from a full set of amino acids. If one essential amino acid runs short, building slows down, however much of the others there is. The scarcest one in a food is called its limiting amino acid.
segments.cue: First box: Limiting amino acid

segments.name: Complete Foods
segments.text: Animal foods, meat, poultry, fish, eggs and dairy, are complete proteins: all nine essentials in good amounts. Among plants, soy is complete, and quinoa and buckwheat are close.
segments.cue: The first four rows

segments.name: Incomplete Foods
segments.text: Most plant proteins are incomplete. Beans, lentils and peas are low in methionine. Grains, wheat, rice, oats and corn, are low in lysine, and so are most nuts and seeds.
segments.cue: The last three rows

segments.name: Combining
segments.text: But their gaps are different, so they cover each other. Beans are rich in lysine and grains in methionine, which is why rice and beans, hummus with pita, or peanut butter on whole-wheat bread give a complete set. They don't have to be in the same meal; over the day is enough.
segments.cue: Beans + grains, then Over the day

segments.name: How Much
segments.text: The US recommended amount for adults is 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day, about fifty-six grams for someone weighing seventy kilograms. Needs go up in pregnancy and breastfeeding, and growing children need more per kilogram.
segments.cue: First box, then More at some stages

segments.name: Found In
segments.text: Good whole-food sources are meat, poultry, fish, eggs, milk, yogurt and cheese, beans, lentils, peas, soy foods like tofu and tempeh, nuts, seeds and whole grains.
segments.cue: Found in

figures.title: Where protein is used in the body
figures.subtitle: Tap a number or a name to see what that place does with it.

segments.name: Where Protein Goes
segments.text: Here's the statue with every place protein is used. Protein is digested to amino acids, and your cells build them back into the proteins that do almost every job in the body. Tap a number to see what that place does.
segments.cue: The statue and its numbered places

segments.name: Digesting Protein
segments.text: Pepsin starts digesting protein in the stomach, and trypsin from the pancreas carries on in the small intestine, which absorbs the amino acids into the blood. The pancreas also makes insulin and glucagon, which are proteins too.
segments.cue: Numbers 2 to 4: stomach, pancreas and small intestine

foodBody.name: Pepsin and trypsin
foodBody.text: Not eaten: your stomach makes pepsin and your pancreas makes trypsin, both protein enzymes. They cut the peptide bonds in the protein you eat.

foodBody.name: Insulin
foodBody.text: A small protein hormone made by the pancreas. It tells cells to take up glucose after a meal.

segments.name: Building and Moving
segments.text: Muscle holds about 40% of your body's protein; actin and myosin slide past each other to make it contract. Collagen gives strength to skin, bone, tendons and cartilage, and keratin makes hair and nails.
segments.cue: Numbers 1, 8 and 9: muscle, skin and hair, joints and bones

foodBody.name: Actin and myosin
foodBody.text: Found in all meat, which is muscle. Your body digests them to amino acids and builds its own actin and myosin from them.

foodBody.name: Keratin
foodBody.text: Hair, nails and feathers are keratin, which you can’t digest, so it isn’t food. Your skin cells build their own keratin from amino acids to make hair, nails and the outer skin.

segments.name: Carrying and Defending
segments.text: The liver makes albumin, the main blood protein, and the clotting factors. Red blood cells carry oxygen on hemoglobin. Immune cells, in the spleen and elsewhere, make antibodies that tag germs, and the brain makes neurotransmitters such as serotonin from amino acids.
segments.cue: Numbers 5, 6, 7 and 10: liver, blood, spleen and brain

foodBody.name: Albumin
foodBody.text: Egg white is mostly a related protein, ovalbumin. Your liver makes albumin, which carries fatty acids and hormones in the blood and holds water in it.

foodBody.name: Serotonin
foodBody.text: Not eaten as such: the brain and gut make it from the amino acid tryptophan, found in turkey, eggs, cheese and nuts.

segments.name: The Leftovers
segments.text: Your body doesn't store spare amino acids. The liver removes their nitrogen as urea, which the kidneys send out in urine, and burns the rest for energy or turns it into glucose or fat.
segments.cue: Numbers 5 and 11: liver and kidneys

foodBody.name: Urea
foodBody.text: Not something you eat: your liver makes it from the nitrogen of spare amino acids. Your kidneys filter it out, and it is the main nitrogen waste in urine.

segments.name: Simplified
segments.text: This is simplified. Every cell is full of proteins, so the numbers mark typical places, not every one.
segments.cue: The caption under the statue

figures.subtitle: The whole lesson in one table, plus a few extras.

segments.name: One Table
segments.text: Here's the whole lesson in one table: the atoms, the amino acid, the peptide bond, the twenty amino acids, the four levels of shape, digestion, and protein in food. Each row links back to its figure.
segments.cue: The table, row by row

segments.name: Worth Knowing
segments.text: A few extras. Protein powders are just protein from milk, peas or soy, without the rest of the food. Collagen is rich in glycine and proline but has almost no tryptophan, so on its own it's incomplete; gelatin is collagen that has been cooked. And scores like PDCAAS and DIAAS rate proteins by their essential amino acids and digestibility; milk, eggs and soy score near the top. That's protein. Try the quiz below.
segments.cue: Worth knowing, then down to the quiz
